item_taken.first_six_words: Quadrat: a grid laid over a
item_taken.why: The case is a grid laid over a territory with the rule that every square be visited, the blank square sent a recorder, and the blanks that survived the visits at the sea and on the private estate are the map of the recorders, which is Quadrat's own illustration in this map and its yield by the form's failure to hold; it is not Monotypic ladder, which needs a hierarchy of ranks and the case has none, not Which end is first, which needs a direction on a recovered order and the case has no order, and not Empty cell, since, as the Quadrat item itself says, a square of ground fixes nothing about what grows in it and can only be visited.

reasoning: The fence rule splits on setting: the form imposed at one setting and what it yields there stay on form-yields; the unit itself and what the same pile yields at a neighbouring grain go to item-grains. The case holds both halves, and its point is the second. The 10-kilometre setting and its yield, the blank as an errand and the surviving blanks as a fact about the recording, are the part that stays, and they are already this map's illustration. But the case is built around the tetrad, the 2-kilometre square that is the named neighbouring grain, twenty-five to the 10-kilometre square, and it states what the same pile yields there: twenty-four blanks per once-recorded square, a denominator twenty-five times larger, a coverage fraction that falls with no record changing, an errand count that multiplies, and all of it closing again when the grain is coarsened. The case's own last two sentences say the records are the same pile at both settings and that what moves is the cell count, the blanks, and the errands, which is word for word the rule's 'what the same pile yields at a neighbouring grain'. The rule decides, and it sends the case across; what crosses is the unit and the neighbouring-grain comparison, and the 10-kilometre setting travels only as the setting the comparison is taken against.
case_out: The unit of the enumeration was fixed by the scheme before any card was returned: the Botanical Society of the British Isles' Atlas of the British Flora, 1962, Perring and Walters, took as one cell the 10-kilometre square of the national grids, a product of easting and northing cut at ten kilometres, in Britain named by two letters and two digits, and a record is a species in a square. The squares that cover Britain and Ireland were the universe; a species' range was the number of squares with at least one record of it, and the scheme's coverage was the number of squares with a card returned over the number of squares there are. Through the 1950s a square with no card was a blank and the blank sent a recorder there, and the blanks that survived the visits, at the sea and on the private estate, were a fact about the recording and not about the flora. The neighbouring grain is the tetrad, the 2-kilometre square, of which every 10-kilometre square holds exactly twenty-five, named by adding one letter to the square's name; the county floras that followed recorded the same flora at that grain. What the same pile yields at that grain: a species recorded once in a 10-kilometre square fills that square and one tetrad of its twenty-five, so twenty-four cells stand blank at the finer grain that were full at the coarser, each a place to send someone; the denominator is twenty-five times larger and the coverage fraction falls without a single record changing; coarsen back to the 10-kilometre square and the twenty-four blanks close and the fraction rises. The records are the same pile at both settings. What moves with the grain is the cell count the fraction is taken against, the number of blanks, and the number of errands.
